Fisher Space Pen Bullet vs TACRAY Mini Titanium Stylus: Which Pocket Pen Belongs in Your EDC?

The Fisher Space Pen Bullet ($35.10 on Amazon) is the legendary pressurized pen that writes in space, upside down, and underwater. The TACRAY Mini ($37.30) is a bolt-action titanium stylus-pen built for phones, tablets, and fidget satisfaction. Both fit in a coin pocket. Only one is the pen you'll still be carrying in ten years.

Published November 2026 · Based on verified Amazon product data and real customer outcomes

Every pocket-pen buyer eventually faces the same fork in the road. Do you want a pen that simply cannot fail — or a pen that does more than write? That's exactly the choice between the Fisher Space Pen Bullet and the TACRAY Mini Titanium Stylus Pen. One is a sixty-year-old design that has been on every NASA mission since Apollo. The other is a modern piece of titanium EDC with a bolt action that clicks like a camera shutter and a rubberized tip that signs your phone screen.

At $35.10 versus $37.30 on Amazon as we wrote this, price doesn't decide it. So we compared the two on the things that actually matter for an everyday-carry pen: writing reliability in hostile conditions, build and pocketability, refill availability, touchscreen usefulness, and what each one costs you when you inevitably lose the cap at a gas station in Wyoming.

Quick Verdict

Buy the Fisher Space Pen Bullet if: You want the most reliable writing instrument that will ever live in your pocket. Its pressurized refill writes upside down, underwater, at any angle, and from roughly -50°F to +400°F — the car dashboard in August included. A single refill lays down miles of line, replacements cost about five bucks, and it's machined and assembled in the USA. It is, functionally, a tool that never has a bad day.

Buy the TACRAY Mini Titanium Stylus if: Your day runs on a phone and tablet more than on paper. The bolt action extends a ballpoint (it takes widely available Lamy-style refills) or flips to a stylus tip for touchscreens, and the TC4 titanium body shrugs off drops, door-frame parking, and washing-machine cycles. It's also the more fun object to fidget with in a meeting.

Our pick: The Fisher Space Pen Bullet. A stylus solves a problem your phone's fingernail already solves; a pressurized refill solves a problem no phone solves — writing when it actually counts, on a wet napkin, in the cold, at odd angles, years from now when the pen has been run over by a bicycle and still works. The Bullet is the buy-it-once choice.

Our Pick 🏆 Fisher Space Pen Bullet — Chrome, Gift Box

Check current price on Amazon

The Bullet is the pocket-sized model of the most famous pen ever engineered. Fisher developed its pressurized ink system with private money in the early 1960s — a sealed cartridge pushed by nitrogen at about 35 psi — and NASA adopted it for Apollo in 1965. Every crewed US mission since has carried one. That's not marketing copy; it's flight history.

What the pressure actually buys you in real life: it writes upside down at 3 AM while you're under the sink labeling a valve. It writes through rain on a cardboard box. It writes at angles a gravity-fed ballpoint refuses to touch, from freezing garage to sweltering truck cab, across an extreme temperature range most pens simply stop working inside of. The smooth black medium-point ink dries instantly and doesn't smear across your palm the way gel pens do.

The Bullet's design is deceptively clever: capped, it's roughly the size of a large lip balm — genuinely forgettable in a coin pocket. Post the cap on the back and it becomes a full-length, balanced pen with a knurled chrome grip. The anodized aluminum body is machined in the USA, ships in a gift box, and a single standard Space Pen refill writes for what Fisher measures in miles of line. Refills are everywhere and cost about $5.

The honest weak spots: posted length is still short for large hands during long writing sessions, the cap (the pen's one moving part) is small enough to lose in snow, and it does nothing with a touchscreen. It is one job, done about as well as physics allows.

Key specs: pressurized cartridge (writes upside down, underwater, any angle, extreme temperatures), smooth black medium-point refill, anodized aluminum chrome body, knurled grip, capped ~1.6 in / posted ~3.7 in, gift box, made in the USA.

📱 TACRAY Mini Titanium Stylus Pen — Bolt-Action EDC

Check current price on Amazon

The TACRAY Mini is a titanium EDC tool first and a pen second. The bolt-action mechanism — the same thumb motion as a rifle bolt, and genuinely one of the most satisfying fidget actions on the market — alternates between deploying the ballpoint tip and the stylus tip. One hand on the phone, thumb on the bolt, sign the delivery slip, flip the bolt, take a note on paper. It's a clever two-in-one that disposable plastic styluses and novelty "pen/tools" don't come near.

The material story is its strongest pitch: a CNC-machined titanium-alloy body with deep knurling, a keyring hole to tether it to your keys, and a weight you forget in the pocket. Titanium doesn't rust, doesn't dent like aluminum, and the finish on these EDC pieces tends to look better worn than new after a year of pocket grit.

The writing, though, is ordinary: it runs a standard slim Lamy-style ballpoint refill — perfectly good, widely available, but gravity-fed. Write upside-down on a wet receipt and it will sputter exactly where the Fisher won't. The stylus side is also a product of its time: fine for phones and tablets with capacitive screens, but it doesn't give you the pressure sensitivity or palm rejection of an Apple Pencil or S Pen on the devices that support them — it's a signature-and-tap tool, not a drawing tool.

Key specs: CNC titanium-alloy body, bolt-action swap between ballpoint and stylus tip, Lamy-style refill compatible, capacitive touchscreen stylus, keyring hole, pocketable mini format, knurled grip.

Writing Reliability: The One Category Fisher Wins Alone

This is the whole argument, so let's make it plainly. Every normal ballpoint — including the Lamy-style refill inside the TACRAY — relies on gravity and surface contact. Press it upside down and ink stops reaching the ball. Write on a wet or frosty surface and it skips. Leave it in a freezing car overnight and the first page comes out faint. The Space Pen's sealed, nitrogen-pressurized cartridge simply doesn't care. It pushes ink to the tip whether the pen is vertical, horizontal, inverted, submerged, or at temperature extremes that would gunk up any other refill.

Who actually needs that? People who sign things outdoors: deliveries, job sites, campsites, fishing boats, hunting trips, farm gates, ski-lift ticket stubs. People who write in parked cars in January. If you've ever scratched a dead ballpoint across a soggy receipt in the rain, you already know which side of this table you're on.

Build and Daily Carry: Where TACRAY Makes Its Case

Fair is fair: titanium beats aluminum as a material. The TACRAY body takes drops on concrete that would ding the Bullet's chrome finish, and the knurling plus keyring hole make it easier to keep attached to something. It's also the only one of the two that lets you sign your phone screen without setting the pen down — a real convenience if your day is an iPad, not a notepad.

But judge the total package. The Bullet posts to a real, comfortable writing length; the TACRAY Mini stays mini, and during anything longer than two lines of cursive, you feel it. The Bullet ships in a gift box and has a fifty-year head start on parts availability — Space Pen refills are stocked in essentially every drugstore and office-supply aisle on earth, while slim Lamy-style refills are an online or specialty-store purchase for most people.

💡 Tip: If you buy the Bullet as a gift (it comes boxed), add a 3-pack of standard black refills at the same time — they cost about $5 each, and a spare in the same drawer as the pen turns a lost cap into a five-minute problem instead of a "no pen for three weeks" problem.

The Stylus Question: Does It Actually Matter?

The TACRAY's headline feature deserves a reality check. Modern capacitive styluses like this are great at the 90% of screen-touching that is signing, tapping, and scrolling — and they're far better than greasy fingertips on a grocery POS terminal. They are not substitutes for genuine stylus ecosystems: if you sketch on an iPad with Procreate or take handwritten notes on a Galaxy Tab with an S Pen, neither pen in this article belongs in that conversation at all.

So the honest framing: the stylus makes the TACRAY the more versatile pocket object, but versatility is only worth buying if paper is your second-place medium. If you still sign, tally, note, and label with ink more than you draw on glass, you're paying $37 for a feature you use twice a week and a refill that quits when conditions get interesting.

Who Should Buy Which?

Buy the Fisher Space Pen Bullet if you want the last pocket pen you'll buy, you carry keys and a wallet and that's it, or you're buying a gift for a dad, a graduate, a trucker, a nurse, a contractor — literally anyone who writes outside. At $35.10 with a gift box in the price, it's the classic move for a reason. It's our pick.

Buy the TACRAY Mini Titanium Stylus if you live in your phone, you want a titanium EDC piece you can tether to your keys, and the bolt action genuinely makes you smile at your desk. Just know it writes like a good normal pen, not like a Space Pen.

Final Word

Fifty years of NASA flight history versus one very satisfying click. The Fisher Space Pen Bullet is the pen we recommend to everyone who asked, because its core trick — writing when nothing else will — is the entire job of a pocket pen. The TACRAY Mini is the enthusiast's fidget-tool answer for a tablet-first life. If you can only carry one: take the one that works in the rain.
